channel.title: Resilience Alpha Research
channel.description: Geopolitical intelligence for investors — one issue every day. Where conflict meets capital.

item.title: Japan Gets the Assembly Line, RTX Keeps the Bottleneck
item.description: Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi announced on October 28 that Japan will host a final assembly and inspection facility for the AIM-120 AMRAAM. The announcement named no site, no partner, no timeline and no output figure. The September RTX contract ceiling is $20.7 billion and the Pentagon said the production increase depends on congressional funding.

item.title: Malaysia Opened the Rare Earth Door by 30 Tonnes
item.description: Malaysia banned raw rare earth exports in 2024. On October 27, DTEC chief executive Milan Perlly said his firm won the first permit under this month's eased rules: up to 700 tonnes of carbonate from Perak, with a first 30 tonnes bound for the United States for separation research.

item.title: A Startup Got the F-16 on the Day Lockheed Got $694 Million
item.description: On October 26, 2026 the Department of the Air Force announced a $694 million production contract for Lockheed Martin's AGM-183A ARRW hypersonic missile, awarded September 29. The same day, Castelion announced an Air Force Research Laboratory contract modification to begin integrating its Blackbeard hypersonic missile on the F-16.

item.title: A 10 Percent Chip Price Cut Costs Korea Up to $100 Billion
item.description: The Bank of Korea, in a written response to lawmaker Ahn Do-geol reported on October 27, modelled chip exports falling by $50 billion to $100 billion versus forecasts if US AI spending slows, on a scenario assuming only a 10 percent fall in chip prices.

item.title: Huayou Paid $71 Million for Ghana's Lithium Seat
item.description: Elevra completed the sale of its Ewoyaa interest to Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt on October 26 for US$71 million in cash. Huayou takes the spodumene offtake and a sole funding path from 22.5 percent to 50 percent of Ghana's first lithium mine.

item.title: The 2 Percent Gas Cut a Prime Minister Answered on a Sunday
item.description: Indonesia cut pipeline gas to Singapore by 31 million cubic feet a day on October 24 and Singapore's regulator calls it less than 2 percent of demand. On Sunday, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong invoked the contracts anyway. The denominator is doing a lot of work.

item.title: The Robots Intel Cannot Replace
item.description: The FCC gave Intel a one-year waiver on October 22 to keep foreign-made guided vehicles running inside its U.S. fabs. Intel told the agency there is no proven domestic alternative, and replacement would take years.

item.title: Qatar Is Now Buying the Gas It Used to Sell
item.description: QatarEnergy signed two contracts on October 22 to buy up to 4 million tonnes a year of Cheniere LNG through 2054. The official word is diversification. The damaged trains at Ras Laffan say otherwise: 12.8 million tonnes a year are offline for three to five years.

item.title: The Metal That Costs $9 in China and $1,150 Outside It
item.description: China defended its rare earth curbs on Japan on October 21, a day after the Financial Times reported Japan is months from running out of yttrium. Customs data show shipments fell 97.7 percent, and Argus puts yttrium oxide at $1,150 a kilogram outside China against $9 inside it.

item.title: 18 Tanker Attacks and Brent Still Only at $110
item.description: The IRGC said its naval mines set two tankers ablaze on October 20, ship-tracker Kpler logged at least 18 vessel attacks in two weeks, and Brent crude sat at $110.38 on October 21. The market calls it a risk premium that talks can remove. The freight numbers say it is already a physical transport tax.

item.title: 25,000 Rocket Kits a Year, With No Contract Signed Yet
item.description: The Pentagon and BAE Systems announced a framework agreement on October 19 for up to 25,000 APKWS guidance kits a year for up to seven years, with a path to 35,000 a year for allies. Congress has not authorized or funded the buy, and neither side named a price. The funded money is older: a Navy contract worth up to $1.74 billion covering up to 55,000 kits through December 2031.

item.title: Twelve a Month: Washington Is Rationing Missiles Ukraine Already Paid For
item.description: Zelensky told Bloomberg on October 18 that the United States now sends Ukraine 12 Patriot interceptors a month, about a quarter of the Biden era rate, and has approved only part of the deliveries Kyiv paid for through NATO's PURL program. Lockheed Martin is raising PAC-3 MSE output from roughly 600 a year toward 2,000. The shortage in Kyiv is an approval problem before it is a factory problem.

item.title: China Just Locked the Solar Factory Door
item.description: China's commerce and science ministries proposed export controls on Friday covering 40 technologies, including a ban on exporting perovskite solar technology and large-scale fluidized-bed polysilicon production. The AI rules got the headlines. The solar rules hit factories already being financed.

item.title: Washington Is Courting the Wrong Address in Myanmar
item.description: Reuters reported on October 16 that US and Myanmar officials met in Tokyo for the second time in a month, with access to heavy rare earths on the table. The deposits sit in Kachin State, held since October 2024 by the Kachin Independence Army, not by the government in the room.

item.title: Taiwan Just Made Chip Smuggling a Crime
item.description: Bloomberg reported on October 16 that Taiwan will add AI servers and advanced semiconductors to its controlled items list, making unauthorized shipments to China a criminal offense under the Foreign Trade Act.

item.title: Europe Is Trading a Sanction for a Supplier
item.description: Bloomberg reported on October 14 that the EU discussed lifting restrictions on a Chinese firm sanctioned over Russia, in exchange for China relieving Sindlhauser, a small German supplier in the ASML chain that Beijing sanctioned in July.

item.title: The Chip Is Now the Border
item.description: FCC 26-50 took effect October 13. A Covered List chip inside any brand of device now blocks that device from the U.S. market. Auditable suppliers collect the premium.

item.title: The IMF Just Normalized $95 Oil
item.description: The IMF raised world growth to 3.1% on Tuesday and assumed oil averages $95.74 a barrel in 2026. Read the internals and the upgrade looks like concentration, not resilience. The Hormuz reopening is already in the price.

item.title: The $2.5 Billion Guilty Plea
item.description: A Super Micro contractor pleaded guilty to moving $2.5 billion of Nvidia-powered servers into China. The controls caught a confession, not a shipment. Three scenarios for what export controls become next, and the P&L line investors should watch.

item.title: The Sanctions That Cost $4.64 a Gallon
item.description: Washington paused its own Russia sanctions for diesel. The tonnage is noise. The OFAC license is the story, and it reprices the whole sanctions architecture. The ticker is VLO.

item.title: The $90 Billion Missile Reorder
item.description: The Pentagon committed up to $6.3 billion for one kind of missile on October 8. It is the third such award in three months, and the three total roughly $90 billion. Demand is not the question. Congress is.

item.title: The Chip Nobody Talks About (That Runs Everything You Use)
item.description: High-bandwidth memory is the bottleneck for the entire AI industry. Three companies control the world's supply. Two are Korean. The third is based in Boise, Idaho — and it might be the most overlooked infrastructure investment of the decade.
